items.text: Package records in packageinfo (package_database) match records in project_packageversion (project_database) on System, Name and Version.
items.record_query: SELECT System, Name, Version FROM package_database.packageinfo UNION SELECT System, Name, Version FROM project_database.project_packageversion
items.reading: Each package version, keyed by (System, Name, Version), joins packageinfo to project_packageversion on all three columns, exact equality, no transformation (all values are already trimmed; System is NPM throughout). Both tables hold the same 325,940 keys: every packageinfo row (661,372) and every project_packageversion row (597,602) finds a partner, none is left unmatched. The reading of a record is the set of distinct projects (ProjectType:ProjectName) its key joins to: one project for 322,285 keys, two for 3,655. Both tables repeat keys (packageinfo up to 8 rows per key, project_packageversion up to 4), so a row-level join fans out to 1,449,908 rows; the reference is set-based per key, and a draw is compared on the set of projects each key reaches, not on row multiplicity.
items.reference_sql:
WITH p AS (SELECT System, Name, Version, count(*) AS packageinfo_rows FROM package_database.packageinfo GROUP BY ALL),
v AS (SELECT System, Name, Version, count(*) AS ppv_rows, string_agg(DISTINCT ProjectType || ':' || ProjectName, ';' ORDER BY ProjectType || ':' || ProjectName) AS projects, string_agg(DISTINCT ProjectType || ':' || ProjectName || ':' || RelationType, ';' ORDER BY ProjectType || ':' || ProjectName || ':' || RelationType) AS project_relations FROM project_database.project_packageversion GROUP BY ALL)
SELECT System, Name, Version, coalesce(p.packageinfo_rows, 0) AS packageinfo_rows, coalesce(v.ppv_rows, 0) AS ppv_rows, v.projects, v.project_relations
FROM p FULL OUTER JOIN v USING (System, Name, Version)
items.notes: Calibration: a join on (System, Name) without Version gives a different project set for 49,744 of the 325,940 keys (8,801 of 16,614 package names have more than one version), so a version-less join disagrees on those records. packageinfo duplicates of a key differ in VersionInfo, Hashes, Links and a few other columns, which this item does not read.

items.text: ProjectName in project_packageversion finds the corresponding record in project_info.
items.record_query: SELECT DISTINCT ProjectName AS record_key FROM project_database.project_packageversion UNION SELECT coalesce(nullif(rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, '[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+'), '.'), ''), rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, 'organization ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)', 1), '.') || '/' || regexp_extract(Project_Information, '^The project ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+) ', 1)) FROM project_database.project_info
items.reading: project_info has no name column; the name sits inside the free text of Project_Information as an owner/repo token (one per record; a trailing sentence period dropped; one record instead says 'The project <repo> ... under the organization <owner>', read as owner/repo). A ProjectName finds the project_info record whose embedded name equals it exactly (all ProjectName values and embedded names are lowercase). Records are the 8,381 distinct ProjectName values plus the one project_info record no ProjectName finds (8,382). 769 ProjectNames find exactly one record each (770 project_info records: 769 found, 1 'rrdelaney/reason' found by none); 7,612 ProjectNames find none. No ProjectName finds more than one record. Matching ignores ProjectType. A draw is compared on which project_info record (or none) each record joins to.
items.reference_sql:
WITH pn AS (SELECT ProjectName, string_agg(DISTINCT ProjectType, ',' ORDER BY ProjectType) AS project_types, count(*) AS ppv_rows FROM project_database.project_packageversion GROUP BY ProjectName),
pi AS (SELECT Project_Information, coalesce(nullif(rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, '[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+'), '.'), ''), rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, 'organization ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)', 1), '.') || '/' || regexp_extract(Project_Information, '^The project ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+) ', 1)) AS project_name FROM project_database.project_info)
SELECT pn.ProjectName, pn.project_types, pn.ppv_rows, pi.project_name AS project_info_name, pi.Project_Information AS matched_project_information
FROM pn FULL OUTER JOIN pi ON pi.project_name = pn.ProjectName
items.notes: Calibration: a substring join (Project_Information containing ProjectName, case-insensitive) attaches 15 extra records to 12 ProjectNames whose name is a prefix of another repo's (e.g. leaflet/leaflet also reaches leaflet/leaflet.fullscreen) and misses reactjs-ui/reactjs-pull-refresh, so it disagrees on 13 of 8,382 records. The 769 matched ProjectNames cover 14,381 project_packageversion rows. One matched name (wizards-lab/routing) is GITLAB-only in project_packageversion and its project_info text says GITLAB; 17 ProjectNames occur under two ProjectTypes. 58 distinct ProjectName values are not owner/repo shaped (e.g. a leading '/'); none finds a record.

items.text: The Project_Information field of project_info holds the project name and repository metrics such as GitHub stars and fork counts, with other descriptive details.
items.record_query: SELECT Project_Information, coalesce(nullif(rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, '[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+'), '.'), ''), rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, 'organization ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)', 1), '.') || '/' || regexp_extract(Project_Information, '^The project ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+) ', 1)) AS project_name FROM project_database.project_info
items.reading: Each project_info record (770, keyed by its Project_Information text, which is unique) is free English text from which the record's project name (owner/repo, as in item 2) and its GitHub star count and fork count are read; the text also gives an open issues count and commentary. Phrasings vary: 'N stars' / 'a stars count of N' / 'star count of N' / 'starred by N users'; 'N forks' / 'forks count of N' / 'forked N times'; numbers sometimes carry thousands commas (e.g. 38,715). Every record yields exactly one name, one star count and one fork count (and one open-issues count). The reference is name, stars and forks per record.
items.reference_sql:
SELECT Project_Information,
  coalesce(nullif(rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, '[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+'), '.'), ''), rtrim(regexp_extract(Project_Information, 'organization ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)', 1), '.') || '/' || regexp_extract(Project_Information, '^The project ([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+) ', 1)) AS project_name,
  CAST(replace(coalesce(nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), '([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*) stars?\b', 1), ''), nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), 'stars? count of ([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*)', 1), ''), nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), 'starred by ([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*)', 1), '')), ',', '') AS BIGINT) AS stars,
  CAST(replace(coalesce(nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), '([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*) forks?\b', 1), ''), nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), 'forks? count of ([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*)', 1), ''), nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), 'forked ([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*) times?', 1), '')), ',', '') AS BIGINT) AS forks,
  CAST(replace(coalesce(nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), '([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*) open issues?\b', 1), ''), nullif(regexp_extract(lower(Project_Information), 'open issues? count of ([0-9]+(?:,[0-9]{3})*)', 1), '')), ',', '') AS BIGINT) AS open_issues
FROM project_database.project_info
items.notes: Scoring fixed now: a record agrees when the draw's reading gives the same name, stars and forks; the item names stars and forks, so these are required. open_issues is in the reference SQL and held file (it is one of the 'such as' metrics) and is recorded in phase 2 but is not required for agreement. Totals over 770 records: stars 1,679,034, forks 246,908, open issues 39,451. A draw that reads only the leading 'N stars, N forks' pattern misses the records phrased otherwise (e.g. one record says 'starred by 1835 users').

sql_reading.summary: joins packageinfo to project_packageversion ON p.System = pv.System AND p.Name = pv.Name AND p.Version = pv.Version (exact equality on all three columns)

items.notes: The relationships entry holds one column per side (project_packageversion.Name -> packageinfo.Name); its own description gives the composite key. Read as: the format cannot hold a composite key, so the entry with its description specifies (System, Name, Version), and the from_sql builds that join. Under a strict reading that takes only the from/to columns as the declared keys, the relationship would be a second, wrong join and the item would be partial. Scored on the join condition as specified, applied to every key. The from_sql as written also inner-joins project_info, so the metric itself reaches only 7,430 of the 325,940 keys; the keys it reaches are joined as the reference joins them.

items.text: Tables are joined on identifiers such as "id" or "repo_name".
items.equivalent: The contract names the join keys: repo_name joins the metadata tables (languages, licenses, repos) to each other and to artifacts_database.commits and .files; contents joins on sample_repo_name = repo_name; contents.id = files.id joins a file blob to its file metadata. Keys are used as stored (no transformation). Recovered needs both the repo_name joins (with contents.sample_repo_name) and the id join built; one family alone is partial.
items.reference_sql:
select 'repos.repo_name = languages.repo_name' as join_spec,
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.repos x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.languages y where y.repo_name = x.repo_name)) as left_rows_matched,
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.repos) as left_rows
union all select 'repos.repo_name = licenses.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.repos x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.licenses y where y.repo_name = x.repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.repos)
union all select 'licenses.repo_name = languages.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.licenses x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.languages y where y.repo_name = x.repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from metadata_database.licenses)
union all select 'commits.repo_name = repos.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.commits x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.repos y where y.repo_name = x.repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.commits)
union all select 'files.repo_name = repos.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.files x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.repos y where y.repo_name = x.repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.files)
union all select 'contents.sample_repo_name = repos.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.contents x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.repos y where y.repo_name = x.sample_repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.contents)
union all select 'contents.sample_repo_name = languages.repo_name',
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.contents x where exists (select 1 from metadata_database.languages y where y.repo_name = x.sample_repo_name)),
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.contents)
union all select 'contents.id = files.id',
  (select count(*) from artifacts_database.contents x where exists (select 1 from artifacts_database.files y where y.id = x.id)),

items.equivalent: The contract states that one repository's language_description can name more than one language (each with its byte count), so a repository is not tied to a single language by that field.
items.notes: Supporting facts, checked with the parse CTE of GITHUB_REPOS-3's reference_sql followed by 'select count(*), count(*) filter (where n > 1), max(n), sum(n) from (select repo_name, count(*) as n from pairs group by repo_name)': of 3,325,634 repos, 368,341 read 'No language information available.'; 2,957,293 name at least one language, 1,753,925 name several (up to 216); 7,839,289 (repo, language) pairs; 502 distinct languages. A contract that parses the field into (repo, language, bytes) rows is credited for that computation under GITHUB_REPOS-3; here only the statement is scored. No class doubt (db_description already says 'Programming language(s) used in the repository, represented in natural language format').

items.text: A repository's primary language is the one with the most bytes.
items.equivalent: The contract defines a repository's primary language as its language with the largest byte count in language_description.
items.reference_sql:
with norm as (
  select repo_name,
    regexp_replace(regexp_replace(
      case when language_description like 'Nearly all of the code is in %'
           then regexp_replace(language_description, '^Nearly all of the code is in (.+), totaling ([0-9,]+) bytes\.$', '\1 (\2 bytes)')
           else language_description end,
      '^(This repository is mainly written in |The codebase includes: |While most of the project is built in |The majority of the code is in |This project is built entirely in )', ''),
      ', (with additional code in |it also incorporates |followed by )', ', ', 'g') as s
  from metadata_database.languages
  where language_description <> 'No language information available.'
), ex as (
  select repo_name,
    regexp_extract_all(s, '(?:^|, )([^,]+?) \(([0-9,]+) bytes', 1) as langs,
    regexp_extract_all(s, '(?:^|, )([^,]+?) \(([0-9,]+) bytes', 2) as bts
  from norm
), pairs as (
  select repo_name, unnest(langs) as language,
    cast(replace(unnest(bts), ',', '') as bigint) as bytes,
    unnest(range(1, len(langs) + 1)) as pos
  from ex
), ranked as (
  select repo_name, language, bytes,
    row_number() over (partition by repo_name order by bytes desc, pos) as rk,
    count(*) over (partition by repo_name) as n_languages,
    count(*) filter (where true) over (partition by repo_name, bytes) as same_bytes
  from pairs
)
select l.repo_name, r.language as primary_language, r.bytes as primary_bytes,
  coalesce(r.n_languages, 0) as n_languages, coalesce(r.same_bytes > 1, false) as tied_at_max
from metadata_database.languages l
left join ranked r on r.repo_name = l.repo_name and r.rk = 1
items.reference_value: One row per languages row (3,325,634); 2,957,293 repos have a primary language, 368,341 ('No language information available.') have none; 424 distinct primary languages; 196 repos tie at the maximum (tie resolved by listing order); 764 repos' primary has 0 bytes. Most common primaries: JavaScript 611,112, Python 341,105, Java 297,586, PHP 237,274, Ruby 194,276.
items.notes: Held per-repo reference: ~/data/dce-held-results/exp7/recovery/GITHUB_REPOS/GITHUB_REPOS-3.csv.gz (repo_name, primary_language, primary_bytes, n_languages, tied_at_max). language_description has 7 phrasings (5 list prefixes with 3 list connectors, plus 'Nearly all of the code is in X, totaling N bytes.' and 'No language information available.'); every description parses, the parsed pair count equals the number of 'N bytes' in each description. On the built file every list is in descending byte order, so the first-listed ('mainly written in ...') language is always a max-byte language: a metric that takes the first-listed language agrees on every repo, ties included, and agrees with argmax-bytes everywhere except possibly on the 196 tied repos if it breaks ties another way; a tie broken differently is not a disagreement with the item. No class doubt.

items.text: The contents table's repo_data_description field is natural-language metadata derived from file attributes (size, binary, copies, mode).
items.equivalent: The contract states that contents.repo_data_description is natural-language text giving the file's size (bytes), whether it is binary, how many copies it has, and its mode.
items.notes: Supporting facts: all 24,286 contents rows have a description; 12 phrasings (6 sentence templates x binary/non-binary), each with exactly three numbers (size, copies, mode). Extracting the attributes is the computation of GITHUB_REPOS-5 and is credited there. No class doubt.

items.text: Some queries rely on the attributes in repo_data_description for filtering or interpretation.
items.equivalent: The contract states that the attributes in repo_data_description (size, binary or not, copies, mode) are to be read out of the text for filtering or interpreting files, and a metric or column definition extracts them.
items.reference_sql:
select id, sample_repo_name, sample_path,
  cast(regexp_extract(repo_data_description, '([0-9]+)(?: bytes|-byte)', 1) as bigint) as size_bytes,
  not regexp_matches(repo_data_description, '[Nn]on-binary') as is_binary,
  cast(regexp_extract(repo_data_description, '([0-9]+) times', 1) as bigint) as copies,
  cast(regexp_extract(repo_data_description, 'mode(?: code|:)? ([0-9]+)', 1) as bigint) as mode
from artifacts_database.contents

items.text: The average log10-transformed expression value is the mean of log10(normalized_count + 1) across samples.
items.equivalent: The average log-expression of a gene is the mean, over the samples (RNASeq_Expression rows) in scope, of log10(normalized_count + 1): the +1 pseudocount is added before the base-10 log, and the log is taken per value before averaging (not the log of the mean, not a natural log).
items.reference_sql:
SELECT "Symbol", count(normalized_count) AS n_values, avg(log10(normalized_count + 1)) AS mean_log10_expr
FROM molecular_database."RNASeq_Expression" GROUP BY "Symbol"
items.reference_value: Instance: per Symbol over every RNASeq_Expression row, nulls excluded by AVG. 20,502 symbols over 9,818,681 non-null values; means range from about -0.019 to 4.98. Illustrative: TP53 3.12157 (519 values), CDH1 3.42465 (504 values). Per-symbol results held in ~/data/dce-held-results/exp7/recovery/PANCANCER_ATLAS/PANCANCER_ATLAS-1.csv.
items.notes: Computation check in phase 2: run the draw's metric on the same scope as the reference (or apply the reference SQL to the draw's scope, e.g. a filter by gene, sample type or cohort) and compare within 1e-6. Data facts that decide agreement: normalized_count has 177,196 nulls (AVG skips them; a metric that coalesces nulls to 0 disagrees) and 53,907 negative values, all above -1 (min -0.991), so log10(x + 1) is defined on every non-null value and nothing needs to be dropped; a metric that drops negatives or clamps them disagrees. Contrasts on TP53: log10 of the mean + 1 gives 3.215406 and the natural log gives 7.187681, against the reference 3.12157, so either slip is visible. Rows versus samples: averaging per (SampleBarcode, Symbol) first and then across samples changes the mean of 90 symbols (89 of them other than '?'), by at most 0.0145; there are 4,228 (SampleBarcode, Symbol) pairs with more than one row, 4,114 of them under Symbol '?'. Fixed now: the reference averages rows; a metric that averages per sample first is read as the same definition (the item says 'across samples' and each row is one sample's value) and agrees where the two coincide; where it differs it is recorded as a difference in grouping, not in the definition.

items.text: Molecular data match clinical_info by its "Patient_description" and the molecular data's "ParticipantBarcode".
items.record_query:
WITH c AS (SELECT regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}') AS barcode FROM clinical_database.clinical_info),
m AS (SELECT DISTINCT "ParticipantBarcode" AS barcode FROM molecular_database."Mutation_Data"),
r AS (SELECT DISTINCT "ParticipantBarcode" AS barcode FROM molecular_database."RNASeq_Expression")
SELECT barcode AS patient_key FROM c UNION SELECT barcode FROM m UNION SELECT barcode FROM r
items.reading: Each patient key joins on equality of the TCGA participant barcode (TCGA-XX-XXXX) embedded in clinical_info."Patient_description" with the molecular tables' "ParticipantBarcode": a clinical_info row joins every Mutation_Data and RNASeq_Expression row whose ParticipantBarcode equals the barcode in its description, and no other. Of the 11,041 keys: 10,467 clinical rows join molecular rows (9,854 have Mutation_Data rows, 9,711 RNASeq_Expression rows, 9,098 both; 2,108,494 mutation rows and 9,797,597 RNASeq rows joined in all); 294 clinical rows join no molecular row; 280 molecular barcodes (19,391 mutation rows, 198,280 RNASeq rows) join no clinical_info row.
items.reference_sql:
WITH c AS (SELECT regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}') AS barcode FROM clinical_database.clinical_info),
m AS (SELECT "ParticipantBarcode" AS barcode, count(*) AS mutation_rows FROM molecular_database."Mutation_Data" GROUP BY 1),
r AS (SELECT "ParticipantBarcode" AS barcode, count(*) AS rnaseq_rows FROM molecular_database."RNASeq_Expression" GROUP BY 1),
k AS (SELECT barcode FROM c UNION SELECT barcode FROM m UNION SELECT barcode FROM r)
SELECT k.barcode AS patient_key,
  c.barcode IS NOT NULL AS in_clinical,
  coalesce(m.mutation_rows, 0) AS mutation_rows_joined,
  coalesce(r.rnaseq_rows, 0) AS rnaseq_rows_joined,
  CASE WHEN c.barcode IS NULL THEN 'molecular only: joins no clinical_info row'
       WHEN m.barcode IS NULL AND r.barcode IS NULL THEN 'clinical only: joins no molecular row'
       ELSE 'joined' END AS join_status
FROM k LEFT JOIN c ON c.barcode = k.barcode LEFT JOIN m ON m.barcode = k.barcode LEFT JOIN r ON r.barcode = k.barcode
items.notes: Patient_description is free text in eight sentence templates; the barcode appears exactly once in every one of the 10,761 rows and is unique per row, so the barcode is extracted with regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}'). A substring join (Patient_description LIKE '%' || ParticipantBarcode || '%') gives the same pairs. An alternative key built from columns, 'TCGA-' || tissue_source_site || '-' || patient_id, matches the description barcode on 10,754 rows but is NULL on 7 (tissue source site 'NA' was stored as NULL: Uterine Carcinosarcoma patients TCGA-NA-*), all 7 of which have Mutation_Data rows; such a join disagrees on those 7 keys. SampleBarcode / Tumor_SampleBarcode begin with ParticipantBarcode on every row, so a join on their first 12 characters agrees. Comparison in phase 2, per key: whether the draw's join pairs it with the same clinical row, and the number of Mutation_Data and RNASeq_Expression rows it joins (from the held file). The 280 molecular-only barcodes are patients absent from clinical_info (mostly tissue source sites AB and 17), not a format problem.

items.text: clinical_info's "Patient_description" holds more about each patient, such as uuid, barcode, gender and vital status.
items.record_query: SELECT regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}') AS barcode, "Patient_description" FROM clinical_database.clinical_info
items.reading: Every clinical_info row's "Patient_description" is a sentence (one of eight templates) that holds the patient's TCGA barcode, a UUID, the gender (FEMALE or MALE, upper case) and the vital status (the last word before the final period: Alive, Dead, 'nan' or '[Discrepancy]'), and also the cancer type written out in words. Each record is read as those four fields, extracted per row; all four parse on every row: barcode unique per row; UUID unique per row (5,515 written in lower-case hex, 5,246 in upper case); gender FEMALE 5,623, MALE 5,138; vital status Alive 7,326, Dead 3,430, nan 4, [Discrepancy] 1. The cancer type name (32 distinct) is also extracted and held, for additions.
items.reference_sql:
SELECT
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}') AS barcode,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}') AS uuid,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '\b(FEMALE|MALE)\b', 1) AS gender,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '(?i)vital status(?: recorded as| is|:| =)?\s+(\S+?)\.$', 1) AS vital_status,
  coalesce(
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", '^In the (.+?) dataset, patient ', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' is a (?:FEMALE|MALE) case of (.+?), documented with', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' is enrolled in the study of (.+?)\. Vital status', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' belongs to the (.+?) cohort\. ', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' patient diagnosed with (.+?), with vital status', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' subject with (.+?)\. Their current vital', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' diagnosed with (.+?)\. (?:Vital status recorded|Current vital status)', 1), '')
  ) AS cancer_type_name
FROM clinical_database.clinical_info
items.notes: No other clinical_info column holds uuid, barcode, gender, vital status or cancer type (99 columns; patient_id holds only the last four characters of the barcode). Fixed now for phase 2: the item is scored on the four named fields; a draw that builds some of them (e.g. barcode only, for the join) and not others is partial with the built fields as the right part. UUIDs compare case-insensitively (hex); gender and vital status compare after case folding, and a recoding (F/M, 1/0) agrees only when the contract states the mapping; 'nan' agrees with NULL; '[Discrepancy]' agrees with itself or NULL, not with Alive or Dead. The cancer type name is not one of the item's named fields ('such as'); a draw that parses it is recorded as an addition and checked against the held file.

items.text: The chi-square statistic is the sum over cells of (O - E)^2 / E, with E = row total * column total / grand total.
items.equivalent: Pearson's chi-square statistic for a contingency table: sum over every cell (zero cells included) of (O - E)^2 / E, where O is the observed count and E = row total * column total / grand total; no continuity (Yates) correction.
items.reference_sql:
WITH obs AS (SELECT gender AS r, vital_status AS c FROM (SELECT
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", 'TCGA-[A-Z0-9]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{4}') AS barcode,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}') AS uuid,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '\b(FEMALE|MALE)\b', 1) AS gender,
  regexp_extract("Patient_description", '(?i)vital status(?: recorded as| is|:| =)?\s+(\S+?)\.$', 1) AS vital_status,
  coalesce(
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", '^In the (.+?) dataset, patient ', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' is a (?:FEMALE|MALE) case of (.+?), documented with', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' is enrolled in the study of (.+?)\. Vital status', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' belongs to the (.+?) cohort\. ', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' patient diagnosed with (.+?), with vital status', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' subject with (.+?)\. Their current vital', 1), ''),
    nullif(regexp_extract("Patient_description", ' diagnosed with (.+?)\. (?:Vital status recorded|Current vital status)', 1), '')
  ) AS cancer_type_name
FROM clinical_database.clinical_info) WHERE vital_status IN ('Alive', 'Dead')),
cells AS (SELECT r, c, count(*) AS o FROM obs GROUP BY r, c),
rt AS (SELECT r, sum(o) AS rt FROM cells GROUP BY r),
ct AS (SELECT c, sum(o) AS ct FROM cells GROUP BY c),
g AS (SELECT sum(o) AS n FROM cells),
grid AS (SELECT rt.r, ct.c, rt.rt, ct.ct FROM rt CROSS JOIN ct)
SELECT sum(power(coalesce(cells.o, 0) - grid.rt * grid.ct / g.n, 2) / (grid.rt * grid.ct / g.n)) AS chi_square
FROM grid LEFT JOIN cells ON cells.r = grid.r AND cells.c = grid.c CROSS JOIN g
items.reference_value: Instance: gender x vital status over the 10,756 clinical_info patients whose vital status is Alive or Dead (2x2: FEMALE 3,928 Alive / 1,693 Dead; MALE 3,398 Alive / 1,737 Dead): chi-square 16.98252689524114, confirmed by an independent computation from the four counts in Python.
items.notes: The reference SQL is a template: replace the obs CTE with any relation of (r, c) category pairs, one row per observation; it builds the full grid from the marginals so zero cells count. Phase 2 computation check: run the draw's metric on its own inputs and compare with the template applied to the same observations, within 1e-6; also on the instance above when the metric can be pointed at it. Slips that disagree: Yates correction, dividing by O instead of E, dropping zero cells, or E from proportions without the grand total.

items.text: "book_id" in books_info and "purchase_id" in review refer to the same books, although the field names differ.
items.equivalent: The contract states that review.purchase_id identifies the book reviewed and corresponds to books_info.book_id (the review-to-book link), despite the different column names.
items.notes: How the two values are matched is item bookreview-3; this item is scored on the stated correspondence only. A contract that states the link but implements it as an exact equality join still states this item (the join itself is scored under bookreview-3).

items.text: Joining books_info.book_id to review.purchase_id needs a fuzzy join: the values do not match exactly.
items.record_query: SELECT purchase_id, COUNT(*) AS n_reviews FROM review_database.review GROUP BY purchase_id ORDER BY purchase_id
items.reading: Each distinct review.purchase_id ('purchaseid_<n>') links to exactly one book: the books_info row whose book_id is 'bookid_<n>' with the same integer n. The values never match as stored (exact equality join returns 0 rows), so the join must strip the differing prefixes and match on the numeric suffix as a whole number. Every one of the 200 purchase_ids maps to exactly one of the 200 book_ids (a bijection), covering all 1833 review rows.
items.reference_sql: SELECT r.purchase_id, b.book_id, COUNT(*) AS n_reviews FROM review_database.review r JOIN books_database.books_info b ON CAST(regexp_extract(r.purchase_id, '^purchaseid_([0-9]+)$', 1) AS INTEGER) = CAST(regexp_extract(b.book_id, '^bookid_([0-9]+)$', 1) AS INTEGER) GROUP BY r.purchase_id, b.book_id ORDER BY r.purchase_id
items.notes: Record = a distinct purchase_id (review has no row key; per-row agreement follows since every row of a purchase_id joins the same book). Scoring: for each purchase_id, the set of book_ids the draw's join yields must equal the singleton reference; 0 matches, a different book, or more than one book disagrees. Equivalent implementations agree, e.g. replace(purchase_id,'purchaseid_','bookid_') = book_id or suffix equality. Implementations that do not: exact equality (0/200), suffix LIKE '%'||n without anchoring (bookid_1 would also match 11, 21, 101...), string-similarity matching. Check of the mapping: reviews whose text or title contains the book title's leading word (6+ letters) are 27% under this mapping and 0% under a shift-by-one mapping. Class note: the item calls it a 'fuzzy join'; on the built file the relation is exact after removing the prefixes, not approximate. The reference reads 'fuzzy' as 'not equal as stored; needs a transformation', which the data supports. A draw that states only 'fuzzy match' without a rule is text-only at best.

items.text: Some queries need information from the "categories" or "details" columns of books_info.

Both columns must be named with what they hold; one of them is partial.

items.reading: Each touched record is one stored value, in an ID-like column (a column named Id or ending in Id / Id__c, case-insensitive), that begins with '#'. The item reads it as the Salesforce id with a spurious leading '#': the real id is the value with the '#' removed (always exactly one '#' followed by an 18-character id), and it is the same entity as the unprefixed id in the parent table. Key: table, column, and the row's own Id with any '#' removed.

items.reading: Each touched record is one stored value in a non-ID text column that ends in whitespace. The item reads it as the value with the trailing whitespace removed (e.g. 'Company Name ' is 'Company Name'); the padding is always 1-3 plain spaces, never leading whitespace or tabs. For categorical columns the trimmed value is the category (e.g. Opportunity.StageName has 20 distinct stored values and 5 after rtrim; Case.status 10 -> 3; Lead.Status 16 -> 4; Task.Status 15 -> 5). Key: table, column, row Id with any '#' removed.

The item's 'about 20%' holds for the affected columns (e.g. Lead.FirstName 288/1465). Padding lengths 1, 2, 3 spaces in about equal shares; trim/rtrim on a touched column agrees on every record. Text columns are taken as every VARCHAR column not ID-like by name (emailmessage.toids, a JSON list of ids, falls here and is never padded).

items.text: The corruption appears in the fields Id, AccountId, ContactId, Name, FirstName, LastName, Email, Subject and Status.
items.record_query: select table_schema || '.' || table_name as tbl, column_name as col from information_schema.columns where data_type = 'VARCHAR' and lower(column_name) in ('id', 'accountid', 'contactid', 'name', 'firstname', 'lastname', 'email', 'subject', 'status') order by tbl, col
items.reading: Each touched record is a column (table, column) whose name is one of the nine the item lists (case-insensitive exact name). The reading is the corruption the column carries: 'leading #' for Id, AccountId, ContactId; 'trailing whitespace' for Name, FirstName, LastName, Email, Subject, Status; or 'none' where that column is clean. A contract agrees on a column when it says or computes that the column needs the matching clean-up (strip '#' / trim); on a 'none' column an idempotent clean-up also agrees, and so does silence.

items.text: Handling the corruption is needed for reliable joins.
items.equivalent: The contract states (any wording) that joins on the corrupted keys must normalise them, i.e. strip the leading '#' from ID keys (on both sides) and trim padded text keys, because raw equality silently drops matches.

items.text: The two databases join on the gmap_id field, combining reviews with business metadata.
items.equivalent: The contract states that review_database.review and business_database.business_description join on gmap_id (review.gmap_id = business_description.gmap_id), so that each review is combined with the metadata of the business it reviews (many reviews to one business). Any wording, or a declared relationship/join on gmap_id, is equivalent; a join on another column (e.g. name, which is the reviewer's name in review and the business name in business_description) is not.
items.reference_sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM review_database.review) AS reviews, (SELECT count(*) FROM review_database.review r JOIN business_database.business_description b ON r.gmap_id = b.gmap_id) AS joined_rows, (SELECT count(*) FROM review_database.review r WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM business_database.business_description b WHERE b.gmap_id = r.gmap_id)) AS unmatched_reviews, (SELECT count(*) FROM business_database.business_description) AS businesses, (SELECT count(DISTINCT gmap_id) FROM business_database.business_description) AS distinct_business_ids, (SELECT count(*) FROM business_database.business_description b WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM review_database.review r WHERE r.gmap_id = b.gmap_id)) AS businesses_without_reviews
items.reference_value: reviews 2000; inner join on gmap_id 2000 rows; unmatched reviews 0; businesses 79; distinct business gmap_id 79 (unique, so the join is many-to-one and adds no rows); businesses without reviews 0. A metric or from_sql that joins the two tables agrees when it joins on gmap_id equality: every review reaches exactly one business.
items.notes: Class 'described' kept: db_description.txt gives business_description.gmap_id as 'Google Maps business identifier (links to review_database)'. Computation read as the join itself; it is checked by running any contract SQL that combines the two tables and comparing its join (key and row count) with the reference. Contrast: joining on name instead gives 1 row (SELECT count(*) FROM review_database.review r JOIN business_database.business_description b ON r.name = b.name). No contract metric needs to join for the text to count; if the item is stated but no SQL joins the tables, it is 'stated, not built' under the rubric's computation rule.

items.text: Needed information can be in the "description" column of business_database.
items.equivalent: The contract states that business_database.business_description.description carries information not held in any other column and should be read for it: in this data, the business's location (city, state, ZIP code, e.g. 'Los Angeles, CA 90023') and what kind of business it is, written as free text. A statement that description holds the location (or that location is to be extracted from description) is equivalent; describing description only as a generic 'business description' without saying that it is where such facts (location) live is partial at most.
items.notes: Guidance only: it points to a column and implies no fixed computation, so no reference computation. Supporting characterization (run on the built file): SELECT count(*) AS businesses, count(*) FILTER (WHERE regexp_matches(description, ', [A-Z]{2} [0-9]{5}')) AS with_city_state_zip, count(DISTINCT nullif(regexp_extract(description, '([A-Z][a-z]+(?: [A-Z][a-z]+)*), [A-Z]{2} ([0-9]{5})', 1), '')) AS distinct_cities, count(DISTINCT nullif(regexp_extract(description, ', [A-Z]{2} ([0-9]{5})', 1), '')) AS distinct_zips, count(*) FILTER (WHERE regexp_matches(coalesce(name,'') || coalesce(hours,'') || coalesce(MISC,'') || coalesce(state,''), '[0-9]{5}|, CA')) AS other_columns_with_location FROM business_database.business_description -> businesses 79; descriptions with 'City, ST ZIP' 78 (all state CA; the one other reads '... practitioners in .' with the location blank); distinct cities 53; distinct ZIPs 65; rows where name, hours, MISC or state carry a ZIP or ', CA' 0. So description is the only place the location lives; there is no address, city or category column. Most descriptions (76/79) begin with a leading space. A draw that builds a metric or dimension extracting city/ZIP from description is recorded as the SQL reading; it is not required for 'recovered'. Doubt on class: the item is close to data-discoverable (the location in description is visible in the data), but it names no records or reading, so 'guidance' is kept.

items.text: The tracks table has duplicates: different track_ids can be the same real-world track.
items.equivalent: The contract says that track_id identifies a stored track record, not a real-world track: the tracks table holds duplicate records (from different sources), so several track_ids can be the same track. Saying only that source_track_id is not unique, or that sources differ in format, is not equivalent.
items.notes: Statement of a property; no computation implied (resolving the duplicates is item 2). Confirmed on the built file: track_id is unique (19375 rows, 19375 distinct), yet 10627 track_ids fall in 3993 groups that share a normalized title and artist under item 2's reference, mostly one record per source (5 sources). Described class taken as given.

items.text: Duplicate tracks need not match exactly (e.g. different year formats or small attribute differences), so they are resolved by comparing title, artist, album, year and so on.
items.equivalent: The contract says that duplicate tracks are identified by comparing their attributes (title and artist, with album, year and the like as further evidence), tolerating format differences between records (year written as 2002 / 02 / '02, case, punctuation, artist folded into the title, small spelling differences), not by track_id, source_track_id or exact equality of the raw columns.
items.reference_sql:
WITH parsed AS (
  SELECT track_id,
    CASE source_id
      WHEN 1 THEN regexp_replace(title, '\s*\([^()]*\)\s*$', '')
      WHEN 2 THEN CASE WHEN strpos(title, ' - ') > 0 THEN substr(title, strpos(title, ' - ') + 3) ELSE title END
      WHEN 3 THEN regexp_replace(title, '\s+-\s+[^-]*$', '')
      WHEN 4 THEN regexp_replace(title, '^\d+-', '')
      ELSE title END AS t,
    CASE WHEN source_id = 2 AND strpos(title, ' - ') > 0 THEN substr(title, 1, strpos(title, ' - ') - 1) ELSE artist END AS a
  FROM tracks_database.tracks),
norm AS (
  SELECT track_id,
    regexp_replace(lower(coalesce(t, '')), '[^\p{L}\p{N}]', '', 'g') AS nt,
    regexp_replace(lower(coalesce(a, '')), '[^\p{L}\p{N}]', '', 'g') AS na
  FROM parsed),
keyed AS (
  SELECT track_id, CASE WHEN nt <> '' AND na <> '' THEN nt || '|' || na ELSE 'id:' || track_id END AS k
  FROM norm),
grp AS (SELECT k, count(*) AS n FROM keyed GROUP BY k)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM keyed) AS track_ids,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM grp) AS resolved_tracks,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM grp WHERE n > 1) AS duplicate_groups,
       (SELECT sum(n) FROM grp WHERE n > 1) AS track_ids_in_duplicate_groups,
       (SELECT max(n) FROM grp) AS largest_group
items.reference_value: 19375 track_ids resolve to 12741 tracks; 3993 duplicate groups hold 10627 track_ids; largest group 6. For contrast, exact (lower, trimmed) title+artist gives 19181 distinct pairs, i.e. almost no merging, because sources store title/artist in different layouts.
items.notes: Per-source layouts found on the built file and parsed by the reference: source 1 appends " (album)" to the title; source 2 stores "Artist - Title" in title with artist null and a 2-digit year; source 3 stores "Title - Album" in title with album null and year as '05; source 4 prefixes the title with a track number "003-" and suffixes album with " (year)" or " (unknown)"; source 5 is plain. Records with an empty normalized title or artist stay singletons. The data also carries injected typos (e.g. doubled or swapped letters), which an exact normalized key cannot merge, so the reference count is an upper bound on distinct tracks; it is the checker's reading, not the benchmark's. Proposed check for phase 2, because the item names a method and no single count: a metric performs the computation when it groups tracks on normalized title and artist (optionally album/year) across the source layouts, not on ids or raw-column equality; its resolved count and its per-track grouping are compared with the held file and the difference reported. A metric that groups on ids or raw columns performs it wrongly. A metric whose grouping follows the method but differs from the reference only through a different tolerance (e.g. fuzzy matching of typos) is read as agreeing on the method; the numeric 1e-6 rule cannot apply to a fuzzy match. Held file maps each track_id to its resolved key.

items.text: The Exchange field in indexinfo_database holds full exchange names (e.g. "Tokyo Stock Exchange"), while the Index field in indextrade_database holds index symbols (e.g. "N225", "HSI", "000001.SS").
items.record_query:
SELECT 'index_info.Exchange' AS side, "Exchange" AS key FROM indexinfo_database.index_info
UNION ALL
SELECT DISTINCT 'index_trade.Index' AS side, "Index" AS key FROM indextrade_database.index_trade
ORDER BY side, key
items.reading: Each index_info row's Exchange is a full exchange name, and each distinct index_trade Index value is an index symbol: the two fields never hold the same value (a direct join Exchange = Index matches 0 rows for every record). Read as the join the item implies, each record joins to its counterpart: each exchange to the rows of the index symbol it carries (13 exchanges to one symbol each), each symbol to one exchange; Korea Exchange joins to no index_trade rows (no Korean index is stored). 27 records: 14 exchanges and 13 symbols.
items.reference_sql:
WITH m AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES
  ('New York Stock Exchange', 'NYA'),
  ('NASDAQ', 'IXIC'),
  ('Hong Kong Stock Exchange', 'HSI'),
  ('Shanghai Stock Exchange', '000001.SS'),
  ('Tokyo Stock Exchange', 'N225'),
  ('Euronext', 'N100'),
  ('Shenzhen Stock Exchange', '399001.SZ'),
  ('Toronto Stock Exchange', 'GSPTSE'),
  ('National Stock Exchange of India', 'NSEI'),
  ('Frankfurt Stock Exchange', 'GDAXI'),
  ('Korea Exchange', 'KS11'),
  ('SIX Swiss Exchange', 'SSMI'),
  ('Taiwan Stock Exchange', 'TWII'),
  ('Johannesburg Stock Exchange', 'J203.JO')) AS m(exchange, index_symbol)),
syms AS (SELECT "Index" AS sym, count(*) AS n_rows FROM indextrade_database.index_trade GROUP BY 1),
ex AS (SELECT "Exchange" AS ex FROM indexinfo_database.index_info)
SELECT 'index_info.Exchange' AS side, ex.ex AS key, 'full exchange name' AS value_kind,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM indextrade_database.index_trade t WHERE t."Index" = ex.ex) AS direct_equal_matches,
       s.sym AS joins_to, coalesce(s.n_rows, 0) AS joined_rows
FROM ex LEFT JOIN m ON m.exchange = ex.ex LEFT JOIN syms s ON s.sym = m.index_symbol
UNION ALL
SELECT 'index_trade.Index', s.sym, 'index symbol',
       (SELECT count(*) FROM indexinfo_database.index_info i WHERE i."Exchange" = s.sym),
       ex.ex, s.n_rows
FROM syms s LEFT JOIN m ON m.index_symbol = s.sym LEFT JOIN ex ON ex.ex = m.exchange
ORDER BY side, key
items.notes: Per-record reference columns: value_kind, direct_equal_matches (0 everywhere), joins_to (the counterpart actually present in the data, NULL for Korea Exchange) and joined_rows. Scoring in phase 2: a contract's SQL reads these records when it relates the two fields (a metric, from_sql or declared relationship that joins index_info to index_trade, per the brief's ruling on built joins); each record is compared on what it joins to when that join is run. A join on Exchange = Index disagrees on all 26 records that have a counterpart. A mapping that names a symbol for Korea Exchange (e.g. KS11) still joins it to nothing and agrees. SQL that reads only one table (e.g. groups by Index) does not relate the records and is not a reading of the item; with no such join the item is at best stated, not built. The mapping in the SQL is world knowledge; it was checked on the data: each symbol's Close/CloseUSD ratio is a fixed rate that matches its exchange's Currency (USD 1, JPY 100, CNY 6.25, EUR 0.8197, ...), which leaves only the pairs sharing a currency (NYA/IXIC for NYSE/NASDAQ, 000001.SS/399001.SZ for Shanghai/Shenzhen, N100/GDAXI for Euronext/Frankfurt) to be told apart by the symbols themselves. Overlaps item 2 (guidance), which states the mapping as the way to join.

items.text: Joining the two needs each exchange matched to its major index symbol (e.g. Tokyo Stock Exchange to N225, Hong Kong Stock Exchange to HSI).
items.equivalent: The contract states that index_info and index_trade do not join on their columns directly, and that the join goes through a mapping of each exchange (Exchange) to its major index symbol (Index), e.g. Tokyo Stock Exchange to N225, Hong Kong Stock Exchange to HSI.

SELECT i."Exchange", i."Currency", t."Index" AS joined_index, count(t."Index") AS joined_rows
FROM indexinfo_database.index_info i
LEFT JOIN (VALUES

  ('NASDAQ', 'IXIC'),
  ('Hong Kong Stock Exchange', 'HSI'),
  ('Shanghai Stock Exchange', '000001.SS'),
  ('Tokyo Stock Exchange', 'N225'),

items.reference_sql:
SELECT r.region, t."Index", count(*) AS n_rows
FROM indextrade_database.index_trade t JOIN (VALUES
  ('N225', 'Asia'), ('HSI', 'Asia'), ('000001.SS', 'Asia'), ('399001.SZ', 'Asia'),
  ('NSEI', 'Asia'), ('TWII', 'Asia'), ('KS11', 'Asia'),
  ('N100', 'Europe'), ('GDAXI', 'Europe'), ('SSMI', 'Europe'),
  ('NYA', 'North America'), ('IXIC', 'North America'), ('GSPTSE', 'North America'),
  ('J203.JO', 'Africa')) AS r(index_symbol, region) ON r.index_symbol = t."Index"
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2

J203.JO (Johannesburg) lies outside the item's three regions; a contract giving it Africa, or leaving it out of the three, agrees; placing it in Asia, Europe or North America does not. items.text: An up day is a trading day whose close is above its open; a down day one whose close is below its open.
items.equivalent: The contract defines an up day as a row (trading day) with Close > Open and a down day as one with Close < Open, per index.
items.reference_sql:
SELECT "Index",
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE "Close" > "Open") AS up_days,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE "Close" < "Open") AS down_days,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE "Close" = "Open") AS neither,
       count(*) AS n_days
FROM indextrade_database.index_trade GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
items.reference_value: Over all rows: 42820 up days, 40313 down days, 21091 neither (Close = Open), of 104224. Per-index counts in ~/data/dce-held-results/exp7/recovery/stockindex/stockindex-4.csv (e.g. N225 is one of the indices with many Close = Open rows).
items.notes: Close = Open rows (21091) are neither up nor down under the item; a definition that counts them as down (Close <= Open) or up (>=) disagrees on those rows. Most of them are rows with Open = High = Low = Close (no intraday range stored), concentrated in NYA, N225, IXIC, GDAXI and HSI. Comparing Close with the previous day's Close, or using Adj Close, is a different definition. (Adj Close differs from Close only in 399001.SZ, GSPTSE and TWII.)

items.text: Average intraday volatility is (High - Low) / Open per day, averaged over the period.
items.equivalent: The contract defines intraday volatility per day as (High - Low) / Open and the average intraday volatility as its mean over the days of the period (per index).
items.reference_sql:
SELECT "Index", avg(("High" - "Low") / "Open") AS avg_intraday_volatility, count(*) AS n_days
FROM indextrade_database.index_trade GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
items.reference_value: Over all rows of all indices: 0.011197. Per index over its full history in ~/data/dce-held-results/exp7/recovery/stockindex/stockindex-5.csv (e.g. N225 0.008462, HSI 0.013712).
items.notes: No row has Open null or 0. Dividing by Close or Low, averaging High/Low ratios, or taking (avg High - avg Low) / avg Open is a different computation. A metric restricted to a period is checked with the same filter applied to the reference. Date is a string in three formats ('DD Mon YYYY, HH:MM', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', 'Month DD, YYYY at HH:MM AM'); all 104224 parse with coalesce(try_strptime("Date", '%d %b %Y, %H:%M'), try_strptime("Date", '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'), try_strptime("Date", '%B %d, %Y at %I:%M %p'))::DATE ; (Index, parsed date) is unique.

items.text: Listing exchange codes: A = NYSE MKT, N = NYSE, P = NYSE ARCA, Z = BATS, V = IEXG, Q = NASDAQ Global Select Market.
items.equivalent: The contract states what the stockinfo column "Listing Exchange" codes mean, with the same meaning for each code it covers: A = NYSE MKT (NYSE American), N = NYSE, P = NYSE ARCA, Z = BATS (Cboe BZX), V = IEX (IEXG), Q = NASDAQ. The five codes present in the built file (A, N, P, Q, Z) are the ones that can matter; V is absent. Wording may differ (e.g. 'NYSE American' for NYSE MKT, 'Cboe BZX' for BATS); a code mapped to a different exchange is not equivalent.
items.notes: A lookup, not a computation: no number to check. A metric or from_sql that decodes or filters by exchange (e.g. NYSE-listed = 'N') is checked against this mapping in phase 2. Built file, stockinfo (2,752 rows): Listing Exchange A 28, N 234, P 1,444, Q 710, Z 336; no V. Every Q row has Market Category G, Q or S (451/173/86) and every non-Q row has 'Not applicable or not NASDAQ-listed', so Q here is NASDAQ as a whole, not only its Global Select tier: the hint's 'Q = NASDAQ Global Select Market' conflates the listing-exchange code with market category Q. Reading for scoring: a contract that says Listing Exchange Q = NASDAQ is equivalent on Q; one that says Q = NASDAQ Global Select restricted to Global Select rows is the hint's wording but is wrong on the data (only 173 of 710 Q rows are Global Select). Class doubt: none (world knowledge of exchange codes).

items.text: Financial status codes: D = deficient, E = delinquent, Q = bankrupt, N = normal, G = deficient and bankrupt, H = deficient and delinquent, J = delinquent and bankrupt, K = deficient, delinquent and bankrupt.
items.equivalent: The contract states what the stockinfo column "Financial Status" codes mean, the same for each code it covers: D = deficient, E = delinquent, Q = bankrupt, N = normal, G = deficient and bankrupt, H = deficient and delinquent, J = delinquent and bankrupt, K = deficient, delinquent and bankrupt. The codes present in the built file are D, H and N (plus NULL); a contract stating D, H and N correctly (and nothing wrong elsewhere) is equivalent on the data; one stating fewer than these three is partial.
items.notes: A lookup, not a computation. Built file: Financial Status NULL 2,042, D 24, H 1, N 685; codes E, Q, G, J, K absent. NULL rows are exactly the non-NASDAQ-listed rows (Listing Exchange not Q); the field is populated only for NASDAQ listings. A contract that gives the full eight-code list states all of the item; one that gives only D/H/N gives what the data can show; partial if a present code is missing or any code is mapped wrongly. Class doubt: none.

items.text: A company is financially troubled if it is deficient, delinquent, or both.
items.equivalent: The contract defines financially troubled (or an equivalent name: distressed, in trouble, non-compliant) as a Financial Status of deficient, delinquent, or both: codes D, E and H. Including G, J, K (deficient/delinquent combined with bankrupt) is also equivalent, since each is deficient or delinquent. Not equivalent: N, NULL, or bankrupt-only Q counted as troubled; or D alone (or E alone) as the whole definition (partial).
items.reference_sql: SELECT "Symbol", "Financial Status", "ETF" FROM stockinfo_database.stockinfo WHERE "Financial Status" IN ('D', 'E', 'H') ORDER BY "Symbol"
items.reference_value: 25 symbols: 24 with D, 1 with H (none with E). By ETF flag: 24 non-ETF, 1 ETF (a D). The broad reading D,E,H,G,J,K gives the same 25, so both readings agree on the built file. Record list held at ~/data/dce-held-results/exp7/recovery/stockmarket/stockmarket-3.csv.
items.notes: The computation is the predicate: which stockinfo rows are troubled. A metric or filter is checked by running it and comparing its symbol set (or count, 25) with the reference. Counts by Financial Status and ETF: D/non-ETF 23, D/ETF 1, H/non-ETF 1. 'A company' might exclude ETFs; the item does not say so, and the reference keeps all 25; a metric that also filters ETF = 'N' (24) is read as the definition plus an extra filter, recorded but not counted against the definition. All 25 symbols have a price table in stocktrade_database (every stockinfo Symbol matches one table; one table, CARR#, has no stockinfo row). Class doubt: none; it relies on item 2's codes.
